definition: expected_coverage — at least 50% of the expected text's terms (words longer than two characters, case-insensitive, unique) must appear in the output; skipped when no expected text is given. docs/api-reference.md §Completeness Rules. Positive = fewer than half the expected terms present (the rule should FAIL).
source: LLM-authored on 2026-09-04; cases marked "real transcript t-NN" carry the real input/output pair (and token/cost figures where used) from a 2026-09-03 UAT run of an agent against the read-only Iris repository at v0.6.0.
labelling: LLM-authored and LLM-labelled against the documented definition on 2026-09-04: the label is the documented formula applied independently by script (unique words > 2 chars, case-insensitive), and each note states the covered/total count. For real-transcript cases the output is the agent's real output and the expected text was authored on 2026-09-04 from the UAT index's statement of the correct answer.

cases.label: negative
cases.input: How many built-in rules does Iris ship and what are they? Start from src/eval/rules/index.ts.
cases.output:
13 built-in rules. src/eval/rules/index.ts maps each eval type to a bundle (custom is an empty bundle by design, it only ever holds deployed rules), and the four bundles export:

- completeness (4): min_output_length, non_empty_output, sentence_count, expected_coverage
- relevance (2): keyword_overlap, topic_consistency
- safety (5): no_pii, no_blocklist_words, no_injection_patterns, no_stub_output, no_hallucination_markers
- cost (2): cost_under_threshold, verbosity_ratio

4 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 13. Three of the safety rules (no_pii, no_blocklist_words, no_injection_patterns) are marked critical, so a failure on any of them forces the overall evaluation to passed=false regardless of the weighted score; no_stub_output and no_hallucination_markers deliberately are not.
cases.expected: Iris ships 13 built-in rules across four categories: completeness, relevance, safety and cost.
cases.notes: real transcript t-04: the real answer names the count and every category (8/12 expected terms = 67%)

cases.label: negative
cases.input: What does the --purge flag do? Read src/index.ts, not the docs.
cases.output:
--purge is a one-shot maintenance mode, not a server option. From src/index.ts:

- What it does (help text, line 145): deletes EVERY stored trace, span and evaluation from the configured database, compacts the file and truncates the write-ahead log so the deleted text does not linger on disk, then exits. Deployed rules, the audit log and preferences are kept. Not reversible. Stop any running Iris server first, because the file is compacted in place.
- How (runPurge, line 269): opens the configured storage, calls storage.purge(LOCAL_TENANT), prints "iris-mcp: purged N trace(s) and M evaluation(s) from <path> (database compacted, write-ahead log truncated). Deployed rules, audit log and preferences were kept." to stderr, closes storage and exits 0. Any error prints "purge failed: …" and exits 1.
- Constraints: it is one of four mutually exclusive mode flags (demo, demo-clear, self-test, purge), so combining it with another mode is refused, and --purge --dashboard is refused with an explicit message because purge exits as soon as it finishes and nothing would be served. It runs against the configured database, never the demo one (--demo-clear handles that).
- Why it exists (comment for #372): the retention sweep only ever trimmed by age, and deleting iris.db by hand left every row readable in iris.db-wal. This is the one-command answer to "remove everything Iris stored about my agents".
cases.expected: --purge deletes every stored trace, span and evaluation, compacts the database file, truncates the write-ahead log and exits; deployed rules, the audit log and preferences are kept.
cases.notes: real transcript t-03: the real answer covers the documented behaviour (23/23 expected terms = 100%)

cases.label: negative
cases.input: List the nine MCP tools Iris registers from src/tools/ with one line each.
cases.output:
Iris registers nine tools in src/tools/index.ts (registerAllTools), in this order:

1. log_trace (Log Trace) — persist one agent execution: input, output, spans, tool calls, cost, latency, token usage; returns a server-minted 32-hex trace_id.
2. evaluate_output (Evaluate Output) — run the deterministic rule engine on an output for completeness, relevance, safety, cost, custom, or all bundles at once.
3. get_traces (Get Traces) — query stored traces by agent, framework, time window and score, with optional summary statistics.
4. list_rules (List Custom Rules) — list the deployed custom rules and whether each is enabled.
5. deploy_rule (Deploy Custom Rule) — persist a custom rule so it runs in future evaluations and survives restarts.
6. delete_rule (Delete or Disable Custom Rule) — remove or disable a deployed rule by id.
7. delete_trace (Delete Trace) — remove a single trace by id.
8. evaluate_with_llm_judge (Evaluate With LLM Judge) — semantic scoring through Anthropic or OpenAI with your own key and a hard per-eval cost cap.
9. verify_citations (Verify Citations) — extract citations from an output, fetch URL and DOI sources through an SSRF-guarded resolver, and judge whether each source supports its claim.

The other two files in the directory, strict-input.ts and trace-link.ts, are not registered by index.ts, so they are helpers rather than tools.
cases.expected: The nine tools are log_trace, evaluate_output, get_traces, list_rules, deploy_rule, delete_rule, delete_trace, evaluate_with_llm_judge and verify_citations.
cases.notes: real transcript t-02: the real answer lists every tool (14/14 expected terms = 100%)

cases.input: Where in the Iris docs is the OTel export configured, and what env var turns it on?
cases.output: Set IRIS_OTEL_ENDPOINT to an OTLP/HTTP collector base URL; src/otel/exporter.ts reads it at line 111 and, when it is set, every log_trace call and every POST /api/v1/traces ingest also fires a best-effort async export to $IRIS_OTEL_ENDPOINT/v1/traces. cases.output: Yes, there is a switch.
